q: Motion along a straight line is called linear motion.
e: True. Motion along a straight line is called linear motion. Motion along a straight line is called linear motion is the path light takes in a uniform medium.

q: In a linear motion, the magnitude of the displacement is equal to the distance moved.
e: True. In a linear motion, the magnitude of the displacement is equal to the distance moved. Displacement can be smaller than the path if the path bends.

q: In a linear motion, the magnitude of the velocity is also equal to the speed.
e: True. In a linear motion, the magnitude of the velocity is also equal to the speed. Velocity is directed. Speed is the size of that velocity.

q: The most simplest type of motion is the linear motion with constant velocity.
e: True. The most simplest type of motion is the linear motion with constant velocity. Velocity is directed. Speed is the size of that velocity.

q: Since the velocity is constant, the acceleration is non-zero.
e: False. If the rate of change of velocity is constant, the acceleration is said to be constant. Velocity is directed. Speed is the size of that velocity.

q: As the body is moving with a non-varying velocity, the instantaneous velocity and average velocity are the same.
e: True. As the body is moving with a non-varying velocity, the instantaneous velocity and average velocity are the same. Velocity is directed. Speed is the size of that velocity.

q: In describing the equations of motion we shall use the vector notation.
e: False. The standard suvat equations are written in 1-D scalar form along a line, for constant acceleration. Acceleration is not velocity. It is how velocity is changing.

q: We will use positive (+) and negative (-) signs to describe the two opposite directions along a straight line.
e: True. We will use positive (+) and negative (-) signs to describe the two opposite directions along a straight line. Signs to describe the two opposite directions along a straight line is the path light takes in a uniform medium.

e: False. The SI unit of displacement is the metre, not the centimetre. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.
